installments.title: Day 1 · Every philosophy is a confession
installments.body: The book opens with a joke about courting Truth and ends up dismantling Plato, Kant, Spinoza and the Stoics — signed from Sils Maria, June 1885. Today gives you the tool the whole book runs on: stop asking whether a thought is true, and ask what kind of life needed it to be true.

sections.text:
Suppose Truth is a woman. Then all those solemn philosophers who came courting her with heavy seriousness were clumsy suitors, and she never once let herself be won. That is the opening line, and the joke has teeth. Every grand system of philosophy, he says, was actually built on something small: an old superstition, "a play upon words, a deception on the part of grammar," or a bold guess stretched out of "very personal, very human--all-too-human facts." Plato's invention of Pure Spirit and the Good in Itself was the worst of these errors, and Christianity, he adds in passing, "IS PLATONISM FOR THE 'PEOPLE'." But he is neither simply grateful nor simply angry. Two thousand years of fighting that error stretched Europe like a bow. He wants the arrow.

Then he turns on the one thing nobody thinks to question: the wish for truth itself. Philosophers have always praised their own truthfulness. Nobody asked what it is, or what it costs. The old riddle flips — we came to question the Sphinx and the Sphinx is questioning us. "Granted that we want the truth: WHY NOT RATHER untruth? And uncertainty? Even ignorance?" He notes, quietly, that there is risk in asking.

Behind every metaphysician (someone who claims to know what is finally, really real) sits one shared faith: "THE BELIEF IN ANTITHESES OF VALUES." True against false, generous against selfish — as if the good things must come from a separate, pure source, never from this messy world. Maybe they are not opposites at all. Maybe the respected things are "insidiously related, knotted, and crocheted" to the ugly ones, even "essentially identical" with them. Our confident rankings may be "frog perspectives" — the view from low down, from one corner.

Why do we hold them so hard? Because most conscious thinking is instinct wearing a suit. Behind logic sit "physiological demands, for the maintenance of a definite mode of life." So he changes the test. Not: is this opinion true? But: does it keep this kind of creature alive? "The falseness of an opinion is not for us any objection to it." Numbers, fixed things, an imagined world of the absolute — counterfeits we cannot live without. Admit untruth as a condition of life, and by that act alone your thinking has placed itself beyond good and evil. The title is not a slogan. It is a description of a move.

Here is the part worth stealing. Philosophers pose as if their conclusions arrived through "cold, pure, divinely indifferent dialectic." In fact the conclusion came first — "their heart's desire abstracted and refined" — and the arguments were "sought out after the event." "They are all advocates who do not wish to be regarded as such." Kant, stiff and decent, walking us into his moral law. Spinoza clothing his thought in mathematics like armour, "mail and mask," to terrify anyone who looks too closely — which tells you mostly about his "personal timidity and vulnerability."

And he is enjoying this. Epicurus mocked Plato's school as Dionysiokolakes: tyrant's flatterers, and in street slang, actors — "They are all ACTORS, there is nothing genuine about them" — while Epicurus himself sat in a little garden writing three hundred books, perhaps out of envy. The Stoics get it worse. Live "according to Nature"? "what fraud of words!" Nature is wasteful and "without pity or justice." Living is the opposite of that: "valuing, preferring, being unjust, being limited." They stared at Nature until they saw only Stoicism in it. Any philosophy that believes in itself does this. "It always creates the world in its own image" — the most spiritual Will to Power.

The same knife cuts Kant's famous answer. How is knowledge-before-experience possible? By means of a faculty. That is Molière's doctor explaining that opium makes you sleep because it has sleep-making power: the question repeated, not answered. Ask instead why we need to believe such things. Then the soul: throw out the soul as an eternal indivisible pebble, but keep the question open — "mortal soul," "soul as social structure of the instincts and passions." And the line the rest of the book stands on: a living thing does not first want to survive, it wants to spend its strength. "Life itself is WILL TO POWER."

Fourteen short sections in, almost nothing is left standing — except the question he has handed you about your own certainties.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: It has gradually become clear to me what every great philosophy up till now has consisted of--namely, the confession of its originator, and a species of involuntary and unconscious auto-biography; and moreover that the moral (or immoral) purpose in every philosophy has constituted the true vital germ out of which the entire plant has always grown. Indeed, to understand how the abstrusest metaphysical assertions of a philosopher have been arrived at, it is always well (and wise) to first ask oneself: "What morality do they (or does he) aim at?"

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: When an argument feels like pure logic, look for the wish it was built to defend — starting with your own.

recall.q: Nietzsche says the falseness of an opinion is not, by itself, an objection to it. So what test does he put in its place — and what does passing it cost?
recall.a: The test becomes whether an opinion is life-furthering and life-preserving, not whether it is true. He argues our most necessary beliefs (fixed things, numbers, the absolute) are useful counterfeits — and that recognising untruth as a condition of life is what puts a philosophy "beyond good and evil."

installments.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

installments.title: Day 2 · The 'I' that grammar invented
installments.body: Yesterday Nietzsche put philosophers on the couch. Today he goes after the one thing everyone thought was safe — the "I" in "I think" — and finds grammar where a soul was supposed to be.

sections.text:
Descartes said "I think, therefore I am," and treated it as bedrock. Nietzsche picks the sentence apart.

Say "I think." Count what you just assumed. That it is I who think. That thinking must have a thinker. That thinking is an activity, and every activity needs a doer. That there is an "ego" at all. And last: that you already know what thinking is — otherwise how could you tell this event is thinking and not "willing" or "feeling"? To name your state you must compare it with other states you remember. So the most certain sentence in philosophy quietly leans on memory. It is not immediate at all. His reply to the man who is sure: "it is improbable that you are not mistaken, but why should it be the truth?"

Then the cleanest line of the day: "a thought comes when 'it' wishes, and not when 'I' wish." Sit still and watch your own head. Thoughts arrive. You do not make them. So where does the "I" come from? From grammar. A sentence needs a subject, so we invent one behind the verb. He compares it to old physics: there was a force, so people assumed a little particle for the force to live in — the atom. Physics learned to drop the particle. Maybe one day logic drops the "I".

Next he opens up the will, which Schopenhauer called the one thing we know completely. Nietzsche finds it crowded. In a single act of will there are sensations — the state you move away from, the state you move toward, the "from" and "towards" itself, and a muscle feeling that begins before you move a limb. There is a ruling thought. And above all there is an emotion: the emotion of command.

That is the trick at the center of today. When you will something, you are both the one giving the order and the one obeying it. We hide that split under the little word "I". So when the order gets carried out, the commander takes the credit and feels a rush of power — and that rush is what we call "freedom of the will." L'effet c'est moi: the effect, that's me. The body, he says, is "a social structure composed of many souls," and the ruling class always claims the wins of the whole country.

He widens it. Philosophers feel original, yet they keep circling one orbit, because the grammar of their language decides which thoughts are even available; Indian, Greek and German philosophy look like relatives for that reason. Thinking is less a discovery than "a return and a home-coming."

Then he refuses both sides of the free-will fight. To be causa sui — your own cause — you would have to pull yourself into existence by your own hair, Munchausen-style. But "non-free will" is mythology too. Cause, effect, necessity, law: useful fictions for talking to each other, not explanations. In real life there are only strong wills and weak ones. And watch which side a man takes: some cannot give up their responsibility, out of vanity; others want to be blamed for nothing, out of self-contempt.

The physicists get the same treatment. "Nature's conformity to law" is not a text, it is a reading — and a flattering one, equality before the law, very modern. Someone else could read the same facts as pure Will to Power. Then the honest shrug: "Granted that this also is only interpretation... well, so much the better."

The chapter ends on a dare. Psychology has run aground on moral fear. Suppose hatred, envy, greed and the love of ruling are conditions of life itself, and the good impulses grow out of the bad ones. That thought gives an honest conscience seasickness. Set your teeth, he says, hand on the helm, and sail "right OVER morality."

Chapter II, The Free Spirit, opens strangely gentle. We live in a simplified, falsified world, and that is exactly how we manage to enjoy it; knowledge stands on a "granite-like foundation of ignorance". His advice to thinkers is not courage but care. Beware of martyrdom — suffering for truth makes you stubborn and theatrical, and truth is not so weak that it needs bodyguards. Better to have masks, a garden, good solitude. "And no one is such a LIAR as the indignant man."

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: With regard to the superstitions of logicians, I shall never tire of emphasizing a small, terse fact, which is unwillingly recognized by these credulous minds--namely, that a thought comes when "it" wishes, and not when "I" wish; so that it is a PERVERSION of the facts of the case to say that the subject "I" is the condition of the predicate "think." ONE thinks; but that this "one" is precisely the famous old "ego," is, to put it mildly, only a supposition, an assertion, and assuredly not an "immediate certainty."

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: A thought comes when it wishes. The "I" arrives afterwards, to take the credit.

recall.q: Nietzsche says a thought comes when "it" wishes, not when "I" wish. So where does the "I" in "I think" come from?
recall.a: From grammar. A sentence needs a subject, so we invent a doer behind the activity — the way old physics invented the atom to hold the force. The "ego" is a supposition, not an immediate certainty.

installments.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

installments.title: Day 3 · Good intentions are only the skin
installments.body: Nietzsche leaves the free spirit's masks and walks straight into the foundations of morality: he cuts moral history into three long ages and argues we are now leaving the one that judges by intention. Then comes his biggest claim yet — that truth may be worth no more than appearance, and that the world seen from inside is Will to Power and nothing else.

sections.text:
Nietzsche opens with youth, and he is not kind. The young praise and condemn with no shading, falling on people and things "with Yea and Nay." He calls this "THE TASTE FOR THE UNCONDITIONAL" the worst of all tastes. Then the turn: the young soul, sick of disappointment, swings around and attacks itself. It doubts its own enthusiasm, treats a clear conscience as a trap, and takes the side against "youth" on principle. The sting comes last: "A decade later, and one comprehends that all this was also still--youth!" Hold on to that word, nuance. It returns at the end of today's reading wearing a very different face.

§32 is one of the boldest pages. He cuts moral history into three stretches. In the pre-moral age — most of human history — an act was judged by what came of it: success made it good, failure made it bad. In the last ten thousand years judgment moved backwards, from result to origin. Real progress, "an important refinement," the first attempt at self-knowledge. But it hardened into superstition: origin got narrowed to intention. We decided an act is worth whatever you meant by it. Nietzsche thinks we now stand at the door of a third age, the ultra-moral, with the opposite suspicion — that the deciding value of an act lies in what was not intended. Intention is only surface, and skin "betrays something, but CONCEALS still more." Intention-morality ranks with astrology and alchemy.

§33 turns the same knife on selflessness. Sacrifice for your neighbour, the sentiments "for others" and "NOT for myself" — there is too much "witchery and sugar" in them. That such feelings please everyone, giver and receiver and onlooker alike, is no argument for them. It is a reason to be careful.

Then §34 goes after truth itself. The falseness of the world we think we live in is the surest thing our eyes can find — but if you blame thinking for that falseness, you should stop trusting thinking too. The philosopher, the creature most fooled on earth, has earned a right to "bad character." Then the hinge: it is only a moral prejudice that truth is worth more than semblance. Nothing could live except on perspectives and appearances. So why demand a wall between true and false? Why not degrees of seeming, lighter and darker shades, what painters call different valeurs? Why not a world that is a fiction? And if you object that a fiction needs an author — why? Perhaps that "needs" belongs to the fiction too. Stop trusting grammar.

§36 collects the payoff. Suppose the only thing truly given to us is our world of desires and passions, thinking being only impulses in relation. Good method says: do not invent a second kind of cause before pushing the first one to its limit. Will acts on will, never on matter. Push it all the way and you reach the thesis: the world seen from within "would simply be 'Will to Power,' and nothing else."

Short strikes follow. Happiness and virtue prove nothing, and suffering disproves nothing: a thing can be true and ruinous. The profound loves the mask — and a mask grows around a deep person anyway, because every word he says gets read too shallowly. §41 lists the tests of independence: cling to no person, no country, no sympathy, no science, not even to your own freedom or your own virtues. The coming philosophers get their name, "tempters," and they will not be dogmatists, since "that which can be common is always of small value." Nor are they today's so-called free spirits, the "levellers" chanting equal rights and pity for all sufferers.

Chapter III opens with the psychologist as a hunter in a virgin forest, wanting hounds and finding none: "Eventually one must do everything ONESELF in order to know something." Then §46 returns the word. Christian faith, in its Pascal form, is "a continuous suicide of reason" — sacrifice of pride, self-derision, self-mutilation. "God on the Cross" was the Orient's revenge on Rome's light-minded tolerance. Why did it take? Because the slave "desires the unconditioned... he loves as he hates, without NUANCE."

The taste he mocked in a young man in §31 he now finds at the root of a religion.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: It is nothing more than a moral prejudice that truth is worth more than semblance; it is, in fact, the worst proved supposition in the world. So much must be conceded: there could have been no life at all except upon the basis of perspective estimates and semblances; and if, with the virtuous enthusiasm and stupidity of many philosophers, one wished to do away altogether with the "seeming world"--well, granted that YOU could do that,--at least nothing of your "truth" would thereby remain!

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The strength of a mind might be measured by the amount of truth it could endure.

recall.q: In Nietzsche's three ages of morality, what does each age use to judge an action?
recall.a: The pre-moral age judged by consequences — success or failure. The moral age moved to origin, then narrowed origin down to intention: an act is worth what you meant by it. The coming ultra-moral age suspects the opposite — that the deciding value lies in what was not intended, because intention is only the skin, which conceals more than it shows.

installments.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

installments.title: Day 4 · The ladder of religious cruelty
installments.body: Chapter III stops arguing with religion and starts diagnosing it — Greek gratitude, the saint, the ascetic, even the busy modern scholar, all read as symptoms. Today holds his hardest idea yet: a three-rung ladder of cruelty whose last rung is killing God, and the first glimpse of its opposite — a man who wants his whole life back, forever.

sections.text:
Unbelief means opposite things in different places. In Catholic countries, losing faith is a revolt against the spirit of your own people. In the Protestant north it is a homecoming — northerners come from barbarian stock and have "POOR talents" for religion. He quotes Renan's warm French sentences, the ones saying man is most truthful when he is most religious, and admits what he scribbled in the margin on first reading: "LA NIAISERIE RELIGIEUSE PAR EXCELLENCE!" Religious silliness at its purest. Then the turn: he later grew fond of them. "It is so nice and such a distinction to have one's own antipodes!" He wants an opposite. An opposite sharpens you.

Then the diagnosis begins. Greek religion poured out gratitude — the sign of a very superior kind of man. When the crowd took over, fear got in, "and Christianity was preparing itself." Gratitude and fear: two different animals wearing the same robe.

Next, the passion for God broken into symptoms. Luther: churlish, honest, no southern delicacy. Augustine: the exaltation of "an undeservedly favoured or elevated slave." Madame de Guyon: a tenderness that quietly wants a union both mystical and physical. And sometimes it is only a teenager's puberty in disguise, or an old maid's hysteria, or her last ambition. "The Church has frequently canonized the woman in such a case." He is not arguing God away. He is reading faces.

Then the key move. Why did the mighty bow before the saint? Not from piety. They saw in that starved body an enormous strength of will — "they honoured something in themselves when they honoured the saint." And they grew suspicious. Nobody tortures himself for nothing; maybe the ascetic knows something, maybe there is a danger. So they feared him too. Will to Power recognizing itself inside its own opposite.

The ladder of religious cruelty has three rungs. First, men sacrificed human beings to their God — often the ones they loved best. Then, in the moral age, they sacrificed their strongest instincts, their "nature"; that is the joy shining in the ascetic's cruel eyes. The third rung is ours: sacrifice everything comforting — hope, hidden harmonies, future justice — and at last sacrifice God himself. Atheism is not the end of religious cruelty. It is its finest form, turned on yourself.

Which explains his answer to "Why Atheism nowadays?" Not new arguments. The father, the judge, the rewarder simply stopped being believable — and worst of all, God "seems incapable of communicating himself clearly." The religious instinct keeps growing. It just refuses this particular food.

Then a door opens. Go all the way down into pessimism, past Schopenhauer, past morality itself, and you come out the other side facing the opposite ideal: the man who wants everything back exactly as it was, forever, calling "da capo" — again, from the top — not only to the play but to himself, who makes the play necessary.

Piety gets the screw turned on it. Superficiality is wisdom, a "preservative instinct." Anyone who worships pure form has once dived too deep and come back burned. Religious men are artists of the highest rank — falsifiers. Piety is "the most elaborate and ultimate product of the FEAR of truth."

A philosopher, he allows, may use religion the way he uses politics or money: a tool. It binds subjects to rulers. It trains self-control in climbing classes. It makes an ordinary hard life bearable, "almost TURNING suffering TO ACCOUNT." But then the counter-reckoning. Left to rule alone, religion preserved what should have perished and worked for "the DETERIORATION OF THE EUROPEAN RACE." He imagines a sculptor's rage over a ruined block: "How you have hacked and botched my finest stone!" The result walking around today: a herd animal, "obliging, sickly, mediocre."

Then the chapter simply stops, and the aphorisms start — short, cold, personal. "'I did that,' says my memory. 'I could not have done that,' says my pride, and remains inexorable. Eventually--the memory yields."

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: Finally, what still remained to be sacrificed? Was it not necessary in the end for men to sacrifice everything comforting, holy, healing, all hope, all faith in hidden harmonies, in future blessedness and justice? Was it not necessary to sacrifice God himself, and out of cruelty to themselves to worship stone, stupidity, gravity, fate, nothingness? To sacrifice God for nothingness--this paradoxical mystery of the ultimate cruelty has been reserved for the rising generation; we all know something thereof already.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Ask it of today, honestly: would I want this one back exactly as it was, and call out da capo?

recall.q: What are the three rungs of Nietzsche's "ladder of religious cruelty"?
recall.a: First, sacrificing human beings to God — often the ones you loved best. Second, in the moral age, sacrificing your own strongest instincts, your "nature" — the ascetic's joy. Third, sacrificing everything comforting and finally God himself, worshipping nothingness instead. Modern atheism is not an escape from religious cruelty but its last and most refined rung, now aimed at oneself.

installments.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

installments.title: Day 5 · The abyss gazes back
installments.body: The aphorisms of Chapter IV run out today, and Chapter V begins — where Nietzsche stops arguing with morality and starts dissecting it like a specimen. This is the stretch that holds the abyss line, and the strange moment where he admits the tyranny he has been attacking is also what built everything he loves.

sections.text:
A criminal, he says, is often "not equal to his deed" — he shrinks it, talks it down, cannot carry the size of what he did. The aphorisms keep arriving like that, one poke at a time, and most of them circle a single suspicion: nobody is in charge inside you.

Vanity is hardest to wound just after pride has been wounded (111). The great moments of a life come when "we gain courage to rebaptize our badness as the best in us" (116). The will to master a feeling is only "the will of another, or of several other, emotions" (117) — a feeling is never beaten by reason, only by a stronger feeling. Even conscience "truckles to our strongest impulse", "the tyrant in us" (158).

Then the social observations, the coldest so far. Forced to change our opinion of someone, we charge him for the inconvenience (125). We never hate anyone we look down on — only an equal or a better (173). Another person's vanity bothers us only when it crosses ours (176). And one line spoken in a stranger's voice: "I am affected, not because you have deceived me, but because I can no longer believe in you."

Four of these have outlived the rest. Fight monsters and take care not to become one: "if thou gaze long into an abyss, the abyss will also gaze into thee" (146). Madness in one person is rare, "but in groups, parties, nations, and epochs it is the rule" (156). The thought of suicide is a comfort by which "one gets successfully through many a bad night" (157). And the title of the book walks past without stopping: "What is done out of love always takes place beyond good and evil" (153). A long series of these aphorisms turn on women, and they are the flattest writing in the chapter — verdicts, where everything else here is a question.

Chapter V then lowers the ambition on purpose. Europe's moral feeling is subtle; its "Science of Morals" is "recent, initial, awkward, and coarse-fingered". Every philosopher so far tried to GIVE morality a basis, and every one believed he had managed it — while treating morality itself as "given". So the real job was never even seen, left "in dust and decay": describing and comparing the many moralities that actually exist. Collect specimens, sort them, work toward a "THEORY OF TYPES" of morality. What passed for basing morality was only "a learned form of good FAITH in prevailing morality". Then the knife: Schopenhauer denied God and the world, halted politely at morality — and "played the flute... daily after dinner".

Next he flips the question. Never mind whether "there is a categorical imperative in us" is true; ask what the claim says about the man making it. One morality justifies its author, another calms him, others let him punish himself, take revenge, hide, or shine. Kant's says: "what is estimable in me, is that I know how to obey--and with you it SHALL not be otherwise than with me!" Verdict: "systems of morals are only a SIGN-LANGUAGE OF THE EMOTIONS."

Do not miss what he does next. He calls every morality a tyranny against nature — and refuses to count that as an objection. Remember rhyme and metre: poets tormented themselves under "arbitrary law", and every scrap of freedom, boldness, dance and "masterly certainty" we have came out of exactly that. An artist in inspiration is not letting go; he obeys "a thousand laws". Centuries of thinkers thought only in order to prove something, and that "severe and magnificent stupidity" trained the European mind. What matters is "long OBEDIENCE in the same direction". Narrow horizons make strength; "stupidity is a condition of life".

The English made Sunday gloomy so the Englishman would hunger for his work again — a fast, and many kinds of fasts are needed; a moral age is an impulse learning to starve and so to sharpen. Which explains a paradox: it took Christian pressure to refine the sex drive into romantic love. Socrates arrives and comes out plebeian: evil is only error, cure the error and the man turns good — the reasoning of people who notice only that "it is STUPID to do wrong". He laughed all his life at noble Athenians who could not say why they acted; then, silently, at himself, settling for "self-outwitting": "follow the instincts, but at the same time persuade the reason to support them with good arguments".

The stretch closes inside our own eyes. The senses are slow and hostile to the new; we hear strange music badly. In conversation he sees a face more sharply than his eyes could possibly deliver — "Probably the person put on quite a different expression, or none at all." We have been "ACCUSTOMED TO LYING" since forever; put politely, "one is much more of an artist than one is aware of." Dreams count too: a man who flies in his sleep will want a different kind of happiness awake.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: As little as a reader nowadays reads all the single words (not to speak of syllables) of a page--he rather takes about five out of every twenty words at random, and "guesses" the probably appropriate sense to them--just as little do we see a tree correctly and completely in respect to its leaves, branches, colour, and shape; we find it so much easier to fancy the chance of a tree. Even in the midst of the most remarkable experiences, we still do just the same; we fabricate the greater part of the experience, and can hardly be made to contemplate any event, EXCEPT as "inventors" thereof.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: No feeling is ever beaten by reason. It is only ever beaten by a bigger feeling.

recall.q: Chapter V calls every system of morals a "sign-language of the emotions" and a tyranny against nature. So why does Nietzsche refuse to treat that as an objection?
recall.a: Because the constraint is what makes anything strong or graceful. Rhyme and metre gave poets their freedom; the artist in inspiration obeys a thousand laws; centuries of thinking-in-order-to-prove trained the European mind. "Long obedience in the same direction" produced virtue, art, music, reason — narrow horizons, even a certain stupidity, are conditions of life. He is attacking the claim that morality has a rational basis, not the discipline itself.

installments.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

installments.title: Day 6 · Fear is the mother of morals
installments.body: Yesterday morality was sign-language; today Nietzsche names what it is signalling. This is the stretch where the herd, the commander who only pretends to obey, and the word "progress" all get turned over — and Chapter VI opens on the scholar who thinks he no longer needs philosophy.

sections.text:
Nietzsche starts with the sky. There are dark bodies near the sun that we will never see; we only infer them. That is his picture of a person. The moral psychologist reads "the whole star-writing" knowing most of it stays unexpressed.

Then he walks into the jungle. The beast of prey and the man of prey — he names Caesar Borgia — are read as sick. Moralists hunt for a "morbidness" in them, or an inborn "hell". Nietzsche asks a flatter question: who gains from that reading? The temperate men. The mediocre. He invents a chapter title for it — "Morals as Timidity" — and then uses it again on moral systems themselves.

Every system that promises happiness, he says, is really a recipe for handling your own passions, sized to how dangerous you are to yourself. The Stoics advise cold. Spinoza kills feelings by analysis. Aristotle lowers them to a safe middle. Art and religion let them out under supervision. Hafis and Goethe drop the reins for old men already past danger. Different doses, one pharmacy, all with "the musty odour of old family medicines". Their real crime is the address: they speak to "all," they "generalize where generalization is not authorized." His verdict is a drumbeat — "expediency, expediency, expediency, mixed with stupidity, stupidity, stupidity".

Now the psychology hardens. Humans have always lived in herds, and in every herd many obey and few command. Obedience has been practised more than anything else, so he guesses it is now born in us: a FORMAL CONSCIENCE. Formal means empty. It only says "Thou shalt". It does not know what. It is a hunger looking for content, and it takes whatever is shouted into it — parents, teachers, laws, class prejudice, public opinion. Read that slowly. The content of your conscience is close to an accident. The hunger is the inheritance.

One consequence: obedience passes down better than command, so commanders run short. The few left feel guilty for commanding. So they deceive themselves and command as if they were obeying — executors of the constitution, of justice, of God, "first servants of their people". He calls it the moral hypocrisy of the commanding class.

§200 offers a fork. A person of mixed descent carries instincts that fight each other. Usually this makes a weak man, and happiness becomes a medicine to him: rest, repletion, the "Sabbath of Sabbaths" — Augustine's phrase, and Augustine was such a man. But give that same inner war self-control and self-deception, and the conflict turns into fuel: Alcibiades, Caesar, Frederick the Second, Leonardo. Same soil, same age, opposite harvests.

Then the sentence the whole chapter walks toward. While a community is in danger, its dangerous instincts — enterprise, recklessness, revenge, cunning, rapacity, love of power — are needed, so they are honoured under nicer names. Once the walls are safe those instincts have no outlet, and the fear turns inward: fear of the neighbour. Now everything that lifts a person above the herd is called EVIL, and the tolerant, self-equalising, mediocre disposition wins honour. Push further and society takes the side of the criminal; punishing starts to feel unfair. The last form of the wish: "we wish that some time or other there may be NOTHING MORE TO FEAR!" Europe has a name for the road there. It calls it progress.

He says it out loud next: morality in Europe now is herding-animal morality — one kind of morality, not morality itself. Democrats, socialists, anarchists differ in tempo, not in instinct. His hope is new philosophers; his dread is man shrunk to "a pigmy with equal rights".

Chapter VI opens on a smaller room with the same fight inside it. Science was theology's handmaid, escaped, and now wants to lay down the law for philosophy — "Freedom from all masters!", the populace instinct one floor down. He half agrees: modern philosophy shrank into a theory of knowledge that never crosses its own threshold. "How could such a philosophy--RULE!" The real philosopher owes a verdict not on science but on life and its worth. To earn it he lives "unphilosophically" and "unwisely," imprudently. He risks himself. He plays this bad game.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: How much or how little dangerousness to the community or to equality is contained in an opinion, a condition, an emotion, a disposition, or an endowment--that is now the moral perspective, here again fear is the mother of morals. It is by the loftiest and strongest instincts, when they break out passionately and carry the individual far above and beyond the average, and the low level of the gregarious conscience, that the self-reliance of the community is destroyed, its belief in itself, its backbone, as it were, breaks, consequently these very instincts will be most branded and defamed.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Before you obey a rule, ask what the rule is afraid of.

recall.q: Once a community is safe from outside enemies, what does Nietzsche say now creates its morality — and what happens to the instincts it used to honour?
recall.a: Fear of the neighbour. With no external danger, strong instincts like enterprise, revenge, cunning and love of power lose their outlet and start to look threatening, so they get branded evil, while mediocrity and self-equalising gentleness win honour. "Fear is the mother of morals."

installments.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

installments.title: Day 7 · Doubt, and the men who command
installments.body: Chapter VI ends with a diagnosis: the doubt that Europe wears as a badge of honour is really a sickness of the will. Then Nietzsche finally says what a philosopher is — and opens a new chapter on whatever virtues we have left.

sections.text:
Say out loud that you are not a skeptic, and watch the room go quiet. Nietzsche notices this and enjoys it. People grow nervous; they hear something far off, "a dynamite of the spirit," a will that does not only say No but PRACTISES its No. Against that fear, doubt is the prescribed medicine — "the mild, pleasing, lulling poppy of skepticism." Poppy is opium. Doubt is handed out like a sleeping drug, with Hamlet as the second dose. From outside the skeptic looks brave and honest. Nietzsche sees a man whose conscience flinches at every Yes and every No, and who has made a virtue out of never deciding. "What do I know?" "Even if the door were open, why should I enter immediately?" These sound like humility. He hears a man consoling himself.

Then comes the diagnosis, and it is physical. Skepticism, he says, is what a certain kind of body feels like from the inside — "nervous debility and sickliness." He traces it to the sudden mixing of classes and races that were long kept apart: the new generation inherits opposite standards "in its blood," the values argue with each other, the virtues block each other from growing, and the first thing to break is the will. Such people have lost "the courageous feeling of pleasure in willing." Then the sharpest line in the whole stretch: most of what displays itself today as "objectiveness," "the scientific spirit," "l'art pour l'art" (art for art's sake) is only "decked-out skepticism and paralysis of will." High standards worn as a costume by someone who simply cannot choose.

He maps the weakness across Europe — France weakest and most charming about it, Germany firmer, England and Spain firmer still, Russia strongest of all, a stored-up will "waiting threateningly to be discharged." And his conclusion is political, not private: Europe must acquire ONE will. "The time for petty politics is past; the next century will bring the struggle for the dominion of the world."

There is a second kind of doubt, though, and he tells it as a story. Frederick the Great's strange father, the collector of tall grenadiers, looked at his clever, French-loving, unbelieving son and despaired that "MEN WERE LACKING." He was wrong. What grew in that son was a harder skepticism — one that "despises and nevertheless grasps; it undermines and takes possession; it does not believe, but it does not thereby lose itself." Doubt with a spine.

Now the distinction the whole chapter was built for. A scholar can be a magnificent workman: take everything people have ever valued and make it clear, ordered, manageable, and so master the past. Kant and Hegel did exactly that. Nietzsche calls them philosophical workers, and calls Kant "the great Chinaman of Konigsberg" — "only a great critic." Critics are instruments, he says; useful, but tools. The real philosopher does something else. He creates values. "Thus SHALL it be!" And notice the honesty of what follows: he does not claim such men exist. He asks three questions and leaves them hanging.

Such a man is always at war with his own time. "His enemy has always been the ideal of his day," and his job is to be "the bad conscience" of that age. Which means greatness has no fixed content — it is simply whatever the age lacks. The sixteenth century was drowning in will, so its ideal was humility and selflessness. Ours is weak in will, so greatness now means standing alone, being different, being "the man beyond good and evil" — the book's own title arriving, at last, as the description of a person.

Then Chapter VII opens and softens into comedy. Our virtues? We are modern; we no longer have our grandfathers' solid ones. But believing in your own virtues is only the old good conscience, "that long, respectable pigtail of an idea" the grandfathers wore hanging behind their heads — and we still wear it. Two suns light us at once now, so our actions come out "motley-coloured," rarely meaning one clean thing. And then the knife goes in: moral judging is "the favourite revenge of the intellectually shallow" on those who are less so. They need everyone equal before God. He says he will take care not to tell them so.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: THE REAL PHILOSOPHERS, HOWEVER, ARE COMMANDERS AND LAW-GIVERS; they say: "Thus SHALL it be!" They determine first the Whither and the Why of mankind, and thereby set aside the previous labour of all philosophical workers, and all subjugators of the past--they grasp at the future with a creative hand, and whatever is and was, becomes for them thereby a means, an instrument, and a hammer. Their "knowing" is CREATING, their creating is a law-giving, their will to truth is--WILL TO POWER.--Are there at present such philosophers? Have there ever been such philosophers? MUST there not be such philosophers some day? ...

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Ask of every high standard you hold: is this a choice I am making, or a costume for not choosing?

recall.q: Nietzsche separates "philosophical workers" like Kant and Hegel from real philosophers. What is the difference?
recall.a: Workers organise and formalise values that already exist — they make the whole past clear and manageable. Real philosophers create values: they say "Thus shall it be," so their knowing is creating, their creating is law-giving, and their will to truth is will to power.

installments.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

installments.title: Day 8 · He is on the side of suffering
installments.body: Chapter VII keeps unfolding, and Nietzsche turns his knife on the gentlest feeling we have: pity. Today he argues that suffering built everything tall in us, that high culture is cruelty in good clothes — and then hands us his own worst pages, pre-labelled as prejudice.

sections.text:
Listen to anyone preaching pity today, he says, and listen past the noise. Underneath you will hear "a hoarse, groaning, genuine note of SELF-CONTEMPT." The man of "modern ideas" — "the conceited ape" — cannot bear himself. He suffers. And his vanity offers him a kinder story: he is not sick of himself, he only wants "to suffer with his fellows."

Costume is the next idea, and it is funnier than you expect. The modern European is a "hybrid" who needs a wardrobe, and history is his storeroom. Romantic, classical, Christian, Florentine, baroque, "national" — he tries them all on, and nothing fits. Then Nietzsche turns the failure into a joke with a future: we are the first age that studies costumes, so we are ready "for a carnival in the grand style." Perhaps parody is the one field left where we can be original. "Our laughter itself may have a future!"

What makes the trying-on possible is the "historical sense," the nineteenth century's "sixth sense." He traces it to mixing — classes and races blended, so every past age now "flows forth into us." We are "a kind of chaos," and chaos has a key to every door. We can enjoy Homer, which polished French taste could not. We can take Shakespeare, that "Spanish-Moorish-Saxon synthesis," coarseness and all, the way you walk enchanted through Naples and ignore the drains. Then the sting: this open appetite is "an IGNOBLE sense." Taste means saying No, and we say Yes to everything. What we cannot feel is finished perfection, "the goldenness and coldness" of a thing that has completed itself. "PROPORTIONATENESS is strange to us." We are riders who drop the reins, happiest when in most danger.

Now the blow. Against every philosophy that weighs life by pleasure and pain, he sets his pity against theirs: "it is sympathy AGAINST sympathy!" You want to abolish suffering; he would rather see it deepened. Why? Because "in man CREATURE and CREATOR are united." Your pity goes to the creature — the clay, the part that must be "fashioned, bruised, forged, stretched, roasted." That part, he says, is meant to suffer, and every human height was built out of it.

Two short pieces follow, almost private. The immoralists are in fact "men of duty," tied in a net so fine that outsiders cannot see it, which is why fools call them men without duty. And honesty is the one virtue free spirits cannot shake off, so they should work at it with everything they have, devils included. But guard it: "let us be careful lest out of pure honesty we eventually become saints and bores."

Then the English. Moral philosophy has been boring, and boredom has damaged virtue more than any attack. The utilitarians plod after Bentham, who plodded after Helvetius, and their real god is English comfort. "General welfare" is no goal at all, only "a nostrum" — a quack medicine. One morality for everyone harms higher men, because men differ in rank.

The hardest idea comes last. "Almost everything that we call 'higher culture' is based upon the spiritualising and intensifying of CRUELTY." The Roman in the arena, the Christian before the cross, the Wagner-lover undone by Tristan — same drink, different cup. Cruelty also turns inward: the ascetic cutting at himself is pulled by the same force. And then he includes himself. The mind wants to simplify, to shut windows, to be pleasantly fooled; it resembles a stomach more than anything else. The thinker forces it to look anyway. "Even in every desire for knowledge there is a drop of cruelty." His task is to strip the paint and read "the terrible original text HOMO NATURA," with "fearless Oedipus-eyes, and stopped Ulysses-ears." Why do it at all? He asks, and the answer trails off into dots.

Last, an admission. Below all learning sits "a granite of spiritual fate," the unteachable — "the great stupidity which we embody." Convictions are only footprints leading back to it. Having said that, he announces some truths about women, marked as "merely--MY truths." What follows — the demand for silence, the sneer at the cook — is the granite itself, left standing in the book with his own warning attached.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: The discipline of suffering, of GREAT suffering--know ye not that it is only THIS discipline that has produced all the elevations of humanity hitherto? The tension of soul in misfortune which communicates to it its energy, its shuddering in view of rack and ruin, its inventiveness and bravery in undergoing, enduring, interpreting, and exploiting misfortune, and whatever depth, mystery, disguise, spirit, artifice, or greatness has been bestowed upon the soul--has it not been bestowed through suffering, through the discipline of great suffering?

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: To know anything deeply, you have to force your own mind to see what it would rather not.

recall.q: Nietzsche says even the desire for knowledge contains "a drop of" what — and why?
recall.a: A drop of cruelty. The spirit naturally wants to simplify, shut windows and be pleasantly deceived; the thinker forces it to see against its own wish, so deep knowing is a violence done to one's own mind.

installments.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

installments.title: Day 9 · Democracy is breeding tyrants
installments.body: The granite chapter closes, and a new one opens on nations instead of souls. Today Nietzsche turns his ear on Europe itself — and hears, inside the great levelling, the machinery that will manufacture its tyrants.

sections.text:
He ends the granite chapter with a threat dressed as a lament. Woman "is unlearning to FEAR man," he says, and the one who "unlearns to fear" gives up "her most womanly instincts" — the "tiger-claws beneath the glove," the "NAIVETE in egoism," the wildness that made a man stand before her "always with one foot already in tragedy." Take that away and you do not get freedom. You get boredom. He asks it as a question: "The tediousness of woman is slowly evolving?" Then he turns and shouts at the continent: "We know the horned animal which was always most attractive to thee." The old fable, he warns, "might once more become 'history'" — only this time "no God concealed beneath it--no! only an 'idea,' a 'modern idea'!"

Watch what he just did. A page about women has become a page about Europe. That is the hinge into Chapter VIII, "Peoples and Countries."

It opens with him listening to music and diagnosing a whole nation from it. Wagner's Mastersinger overture has "fire and courage," yes — and also "the loose, dun-coloured skin of fruits which ripen too late." No South, no grace, no dance. From one overture he draws the sentence the chapter hangs on: the Germans "belong to the day before yesterday and the day after tomorrow--THEY HAVE AS YET NO TODAY."

Then the honest move. He calls himself a "good European," and admits he has just caught himself in "a plunge and relapse into old loves and narrow views--I have just given an example of it." That is the method here: let the patriotic warmth rise, then ask what it is made of.

He stages the answer as comedy. Two old patriots, both deaf, shout at each other. One says: a statesman who forces a people into "high politics" they were never built for, who narrows their minds and makes their taste "national," is not great. The other shouts back, "Undoubtedly!... otherwise he COULD NOT have done it!" Strong is not great, the first insists. Nietzsche listens "in my happiness and apartness" and thinks what neither deaf man can hear: "how soon a stronger one may become master of the strong."

Which sets up the coldest page of the day. Call it civilization, humanising, progress, democracy — underneath all those words, he says, runs "an immense PHYSIOLOGICAL PROCESS," a change in bodies, not in opinions. Europeans are mixing, loosening from climate and soil, becoming "an essentially SUPER-NATIONAL and nomadic species" whose one great skill is adapting. The average result: "numerous, talkative, weak-willed, and very handy workmen who REQUIRE a master, a commander, as they require their daily bread." But the same conditions — wide schooling, endless practice, the habit of disguise — make the rare exception stronger than any before him. So: "the democratising of Europe is at the same time an involuntary arrangement for the rearing of TYRANTS."

The rest of the day is Nietzsche turning his taste on his own country. German "depth," he suspects, is only slow digestion: "he digests his events badly; he never gets 'done' with them." German honesty is a costume, and a useful one — better to keep posing as "profound, clumsy, good-natured, honest, and foolish." Mozart is the last echo of a whole European taste; Schumann, a "noble weakling," is where German music began "LOSING THE VOICE FOR THE SOUL OF EUROPE."

Then two short sections that quietly tell you how to read him. A sentence has a tempo, like music; miss the tempo and "the sentence itself is misunderstood." The ancients read out loud, so a sentence was "a physiological whole, inasmuch as it is comprised in one breath." We cannot manage it: "WE have really no right to the BIG period, we modern men, who are short of breath in every sense!"

He ends the run on a note you do not expect. What does Europe owe to the Jews? "The grand style in morality, the fearfulness and majesty of infinite demands" — the seriousness that makes moral questions feel enormous at all. For this, he writes, "we artists among the spectators and philosophers, are--grateful to the Jews." It is the one clean gratitude in the chapter.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: while, therefore, the democratising of Europe will tend to the production of a type prepared for SLAVERY in the most subtle sense of the term: the STRONG man will necessarily in individual and exceptional cases, become stronger and richer than he has perhaps ever been before--owing to the unprejudicedness of his schooling, owing to the immense variety of practice, art, and disguise. I meant to say that the democratising of Europe is at the same time an involuntary arrangement for the rearing of TYRANTS--taking the word in all its meanings, even in its most spiritual sense.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: An age that trains everyone to adapt is training most of them to obey — and a few to rule.

recall.q: Why does Nietzsche call the democratising of Europe an "involuntary arrangement for the rearing of TYRANTS"?
recall.a: Because the same conditions produce both halves at once. The average European becomes adaptable, talkative, weak-willed — a handy workman who needs a master the way he needs bread. But that wide schooling, endless practice and habit of disguise also make the rare exception stronger and richer than ever. Levelling does not remove the commander; it creates the appetite for one, and sharpens the few who can be it.

installments.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

installments.title: Day 10 · Two moralities in one soul
installments.body: Nietzsche spends four sections insulting England, praising France, and dreaming of music with no morals left in it — then opens Chapter IX and finally says what "noble" means. Today the book snaps into focus: values were made in two different places, by two different kinds of people, and both are still fighting inside you.

sections.text:
He opens by settling a score with England. The English are "not a philosophical race." Bacon attacked the philosophical spirit; Hobbes, Hume and Locke dragged down what the word "philosopher" even means. Then the attack turns physical. The Englishman is "more gloomy, sensual, headstrong, and brutal" than the German, and for that very reason needs Christianity more — it is the discipline that moralizes him, "the finer poison to neutralize the coarser." Under the rudeness sits a real claim: a people's religion fits the shape of its appetites. His final complaint is the deepest insult he owns. The Englishman has "neither rhythm nor dance in the movements of his soul and body." No music.

Then a thought that stings much wider than England. Some truths are best found by mediocre minds, because those truths suit such minds. He names Darwin, Mill, Spencer — patient collectors of "many little common facts." The high, independent mind is actually bad at that work, because it has different work: "they have to BE something new... they have to REPRESENT new values!" And then the line that should trouble any clever reader: "the capable man in the grand style, the creator, will possibly have to be an ignorant person." Knowing and making are two separate powers, and the gap between them is wider than we think.

France gets the opposite verdict. It is still "the high school of taste," though the few who carry that taste keep themselves well hidden. Three things are France's own: devotion to form; centuries of moralistic work, which leaves even a newspaper novelist with a psychological sensitiveness Germany has no conception of; and a half-way mix of North and South. Then he drops the argument and simply longs. He wants a music freed from the North — "super-German," even super-European, at home with "big, beautiful, lonely beasts of prey." And under all the nationalist noise he sees one fact: the deepest men of the century were quietly preparing "the European of the future." Napoleon, Goethe, Beethoven, Stendhal, Heine, Schopenhauer. They only rested from themselves when they became "patriots."

Chapter IX opens: What is Noble? The answer begins brutally. Every rise in the type "man" has been the work of an aristocratic society — one that believes in rank, and needs slavery "in some form or other." The mechanism has a name: the PATHOS OF DISTANCE. Long practice of looking down and looking up, of commanding and obeying, builds a gap between classes; that outer gap is then copied inward as "the longing for an ever new widening of distance within the soul itself." Distance from others teaches distance from yourself. That, he says, is how a soul grows taller. And he refuses the flattering version of history: the first noble caste was always the barbarian caste, men of prey falling on gentler, more peaceful people.

He pushes harder. A healthy aristocracy does not see itself as a function of society; society is its scaffolding — like the climbing plant in Java that wraps an oak until it can open its top in the light. And making "injure no one" the basic rule of society would be "a Will to the DENIAL of life," because living is appropriation, conquest, exploitation. Not as a crime. As an organic function, like digestion.

Which sets up the map. Moral values were invented in two places. Among rulers, "good" simply means noble and "bad" means despicable. The noble man is "a CREATOR OF VALUES": he needs no approval, he confers honour on things, his morality is self-glorification. He helps the unfortunate — but out of overflowing power, not pity. He has duties only to equals. "Wotan placed a hard heart in my breast."

Then Nietzsche turns and asks the other question. Suppose the abused, the oppressed, the weary and the uncertain begin to moralize. What will they call good?

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: I could imagine a music of which the rarest charm would be that it knew nothing more of good and evil; only that here and there perhaps some sailor's home-sickness, some golden shadows and tender weaknesses might sweep lightly over it; an art which, from the far distance, would see the colours of a sinking and almost incomprehensible MORAL world fleeing towards it, and would be hospitable enough and profound enough to receive such belated fugitives.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Every value has a birthplace. Ask whether it was made by someone overflowing, or by someone suffering.

recall.q: How do master-morality and slave-morality begin differently?
recall.a: Master-morality begins inside the ruler: he calls his own proud qualities "good" and everything unlike them "bad" — noble versus despicable. He is a creator of values who needs nobody's approval. Slave-morality begins from the outside, among the oppressed and suffering, as suspicion of the powerful and distrust of what they call good.

installments.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

installments.title: Day 11 · Mediocrity wins, so the rare wear masks
installments.body: Yesterday gave us master and slave morality as two types. Today Nietzsche shows the machine that builds a noble type, the peace that dissolves it, and then follows the rare soul down into its ancestry, its loneliness, and its masks.

sections.text:
Start with breeders, he says. A type becomes hard only through "the long struggle with essentially constant UNFAVOURABLE conditions." Give a species too much food and too much protection and it goes strange — "fertile in prodigies and monstrosities." Now look at an old Greek city, or Venice: machines for "REARING human beings." Men stand side by side with no safety net. They must prevail "or else run the terrible danger of being exterminated." Whatever kept them alive they call virtues, and only those they bring to maturity. Severely. Aristocratic morality is intolerant about youth, women, marriage, punishment — and it counts intolerance itself as a virtue, "under the name of 'justice.'"

Then the good years come. The neighbours stop attacking; food is everywhere. "With one stroke the bond and constraint of the old discipline severs." The discipline can continue only as "a form of LUXURY, as an archaizing TASTE." Everything bursts out at once: deviations "into the higher, finer, and rarer," and also monsters. "The individual dares to be individual and detach himself." He calls this a "TROPICAL TEMPO" of growth tangled with self-destruction, "a portentous simultaneousness of Spring and Autumn." The old morality piled up all this strength. It "bent the bow." Now it is out of date.

Then the turn that makes this section great. Danger returns — danger is "the mother of morality" — but now it lives inside: in the neighbour, in the street, "into their own child, into their own heart." The moral philosophers of such an age look around and see one fact. Only one type will still be here the day after tomorrow: "the incurably MEDIOCRE." So the only morality with a future, the only one that still gets a hearing, is "be like them! become mediocre!" It can never admit that. It must speak of "moderation and dignity and duty and brotherly love." It "will have difficulty IN CONCEALING ITS IRONY!"

From there he tests individual souls, and his instrument is reverence. Put something genuinely high in front of a person while it is still unknown and unprotected, then watch. In a common nature the vulgarity "spurts up suddenly like dirty water." In a fine one the gestures stop and the eye hesitates. Here he pays Christianity a compliment: guarding the Bible taught the masses "that they are not allowed to touch everything." He finds more tact for reverence among peasants than among the "newspaper-reading DEMIMONDE of intellect." And ancestors cannot be scrubbed out; modern education is largely "the art of deceiving" about origin.

He lets the noble soul keep its egoism without apology. It feels no harshness in itself; it would call itself "justice itself." Among equals it turns careful and delicate, because "every star is a similar egoist" — it honours itself in them. It looks forward or down, rarely up: "HE KNOWS THAT HE IS ON A HEIGHT." Modern life's motto, by contrast, is a Chinese proverb mothers teach their children: "SIAO-SIN," make thy heart small.

Then the mechanism of flattening. Words stand for shared sensations, so understanding each other needs shared experience; danger makes quick agreement urgent; therefore "the history of language is the history of a process of abbreviation." The ordinary always wins. The rare "succumb to accidents in their isolation, and seldom propagate themselves." That slow drift to the average is the drift "to the IGNOBLE."

And the man who sees all this pays for it. The psychologist who studies rare souls risks "being suffocated by sympathy," because their ruin is the rule, not the exception. He watches crowds worship "great men" where he has perceived: "SUCCESS has always been the greatest liar." Even love, which women trust to fix everything, "rather DESTROYS than saves." So the rare hide. Gaiety, science, even foolishness become disguises — which is why the wanderer, offered anything at all to refresh him, asks for one thing only: "Another mask! A second mask!"

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: Profound suffering makes noble: it separates.--One of the most refined forms of disguise is Epicurism, along with a certain ostentatious boldness of taste, which takes suffering lightly, and puts itself on the defensive against all that is sorrowful and profound. They are "gay men" who make use of gaiety, because they are misunderstood on account of it--they WISH to be misunderstood. There are "scientific minds" who make use of science, because it gives a gay appearance, and because scientificness leads to the conclusion that a person is superficial--they WISH to mislead to a false conclusion.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: What lasts is not what is highest — which is why the rare learn to wear masks.

recall.q: In §262, what happens to a hard aristocratic morality once the danger it was built for disappears — and what morality replaces it?
recall.a: The old discipline snaps in one stroke and survives only as luxury or old-fashioned taste. Growth and decay explode together, "Spring and Autumn" at once, and since only "the incurably MEDIOCRE" can survive such a time, the one morality still heard is "become mediocre!" — preached in the safe language of moderation, dignity, duty and brotherly love.

installments.attribution: Friedrich Nietzsche · Helen Zimmern tr. · public domain

installments.title: Day 12 · The mask, the laugh, the farewell
installments.body: The book ends here, and it ends by explaining itself: books are written to hide what is in us, every word is a mask, and behind every cave in a man there is a deeper cave. Then Nietzsche names the god he has been serving all along, laughs at everything serious, says goodbye to his own thoughts, and calls out for new friends.

sections.text:
Some people cannot hide that they are clever. They twist, they cover their eyes with a hand — "as though the hand were not a betrayer" — and it still shows. So Nietzsche offers the best disguise he knows, and it is a joke with a blade in it: enthusiasm. Be warm, be loud, be full of virtue, and people will file you under harmless. He borrows Galiani's line, from a man "who was obliged to know it": VERTU EST ENTHOUSIASME. Virtue is enthusiasm.

Then comes the passage that explains the whole book. He describes how a recluse's writing sounds. A man who has sat alone with his soul "from year's end to year's end" becomes "a cave-bear, or a treasure-seeker, or a treasure-guardian and dragon in his cave," and his ideas take on a twilight colour and a smell of mould. Such a man does not believe that books tell the truth about their author: "are not books written precisely to hide what is in us?" He goes further. He doubts a philosopher can have final opinions at all, because "behind every cave in him" there is a still deeper cave, an abyss under every bottom. So every philosophy is a front. The thinker stopped digging somewhere and called that spot the foundation — and the stopping was arbitrary, and "there is also something suspicious in it." Every opinion is a hiding place. Every word is a mask. His own words too, which is the trap and the gift of reading him.

Why hide? The next line gives a reason you may not expect. "Every deep thinker is more afraid of being understood than of being misunderstood." Misunderstanding only wounds vanity. Being understood wounds the heart, because now another person has to carry what you carry: "Ah, why would you also have as hard a time of it as I have?" The mask is partly mercy.

Then the psychology under everything. Man is a "COMPLEX, mendacious, artful, and inscrutable animal," frightening to other animals for his cunning, not his strength. And this tangled creature invented the good conscience so that he could finally enjoy his own soul "as something SIMPLE." Morality is therefore "a long, audacious falsification" — a paint job that makes looking at yourself bearable. Which means there is more art inside morality than we admit.

A philosopher, he adds, is a man struck by his own thoughts "as if they came from the outside," like lightning; a man who runs away from himself and whose curiosity keeps dragging him back. Two dislikes follow. Europe has built "a regular cult of suffering" — complaint dressed up as something noble; sympathy is worth something from a man who could also punish, and little from those who only suffer. Against it he prescribes an amulet for the neck: "GAI SABER," gay science. And he ranks philosophers by the quality of their laughing, up to those capable of "GOLDEN laughter." Hobbes called laughing a defect to overcome; Nietzsche thinks the gods laugh, even in holy matters.

Then the mask lifts. He praises a spirit with "the genius of the heart," who leaves everyone richer, "broken up, blown upon," "full of hopes which as yet lack names" — and at last gives the name: Dionysus. The god says he likes man and wants to make him "stronger, more evil, and more profound." Nietzsche asks it back in horror; the god repeats it, adds "also more beautiful," and smiles. Then the dry last word on gods: "We men are--more human."

He closes by turning on his own pages. His thoughts were young and malicious, full of thorns — now some of them look "ready to become truths," honest and tedious. We only catch what is already tired enough to be caught. The final poem is midday on a cold ridge: old friends stare at him and go pale, he asks "I am not I?", and he stands there calling for new ones. Zarathustra arrives, the grisly veil tears, and the world laughs.

sections.label: From the book
sections.text: Alas! what are you, after all, my written and painted thoughts! Not long ago you were so variegated, young and malicious, so full of thorns and secret spices, that you made me sneeze and laugh--and now? You have already doffed your novelty, and some of you, I fear, are ready to become truths, so immortal do they look, so pathetically honest, so tedious!

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Wherever you stopped digging, you called it the foundation. That was a choice, not a floor.

recall.q: Nietzsche calls every philosophy a "foreground philosophy." What does he mean by that?
recall.a: That a book hides more of its author than it shows. Behind every cave in a man there is a deeper cave, so wherever a philosopher laid his spade aside and called that spot the foundation was arbitrary — and a little suspicious. Every opinion is a lurking-place; every word is also a mask.
